articles.title: Dialogue King Sai Kumar Birthday Special
articles.description: Sai Kumar is a name that needs no introduction to Telugu audiences. The moment his name is mentioned, what comes to mind is his powerful baritone, impeccable diction, and commanding dialogue delivery. Having lent his iconic voice to numerous leading actors, he went on to establish himself as a celebrated actor in his own right. It is no surprise that the Telugu film industry fondly honours him with the title "Dialogue King." Born on July 27, 1961, Sai Kumar hails from a distinguished film family as the son of veteran actor P. J. Sharma. Despite his cinematic background, he carved his own identity through sheer talent and dedication. Recently, he achieved the remarkable milestone of completing 50 glorious years in the film industry. Sai Kumar began his career as a dubbing artist, lending his powerful voice to heroes and several prominent characters in numerous films. His first dubbing assignment was for the film Samsaram. He later made his debut as a child actor with Devudu Chesina Pelli. However, it was the Kannada blockbuster Police Story that catapulted him to stardom. The film's dubbed Telugu version also became a massive hit, earning him immense popularity among Telugu audiences. Over the years, Sai Kumar has enjoyed an illustrious career across Telugu, Kannada, and Tamil cinema, excelling as a hero, villain, and character actor. Whether portraying a fearless police officer, an emotional father, or a powerful antagonist, he has consistently impressed audiences with his remarkable versatility and screen presence. Even in his second innings, Sai Kumar continues to stay busier than ever with an exciting lineup of projects. He is playing pivotal roles in Ravi Teja's Irumudi, Dharmasthala Niyojakavargam, Sambarala Yetigattu, Nagarjuna's landmark 100th film, S. V. Krishna Reddy's Vedavyas, a film directed by Kiran Abbavaram, Roshan Meka's Emo Emo Idi, a Vishwak Sen starrer, Siddhu Jonnalagadda's Lungi Man, the Nithiin–Nani project, Satyadev's Full Bottle, Varun Tej's Bari, Varalaxmi Sarathkumar's Kurmavataram, and Sai Prakash's Sai Baba. He will also make a special appearance in Ashwin Babu's Vachinavadu Goutham and a cameo in Aadi Sai Kumar's SI Yugandhar. Apart from films, Sai Kumar is also part of Moodu Lantharlu, starring Aishwarya Rajesh, and the web series Kanyasulkam. In Kannada, he is playing significant roles in Shivarajkumar's Bail, Nirup Bhandari's Satya: Son of Harishchandra, and Kichcha Sudeep's Billa Ranga Baasha. From being one of India's finest dubbing artists to becoming a successful hero and one of the most respected character actors, Sai Kumar has left an indelible mark on Indian cinema. As he continues to entertain audiences with memorable performances, we wish the Dialogue King good health, happiness, and many more years of cinematic excellence. *Happy Birthday, Dialogue King Sai Kumar!*

articles.title: Alia Bhatt, Katrina Kaif And Kareena Kapoor Are Obsessed With Bandanas—Here's Why
articles.description:
Bandanas are enjoying another fashion revival, with celebrities including Priyanka Chopra, Alia Bhatt, Katrina Kaif, Kiara Advani, Kareena Kapoor and Ananya Panday styling them in very different ways. While the accessory looks modern on runways and social media, its story stretches back centuries. Its origins lie in India's traditional textile craftsmanship before it travelled across continents through trade. Over time, the simple square of fabric evolved into much more than a style statement. It became a symbol of identity, resistance, empowerment and cultural pride, proving that one of fashion's most popular accessories also carries a remarkable history that deserves attention today.

Bandana Origins

From Indian Craftsmanship To Global Fashion

The bandana traces its roots to India, where artisans created colourful fabrics using the traditional Bandhani tie-and-dye technique. The name is widely believed to come from the Sanskrit word badhnati, meaning "to tie", or from Bandhani itself. According to historians, the familiar paisley-style pattern also reflects the ancient Persian boteh motif, a design linked to life and eternity. During the 18th century, the British East India Company exported these textiles to Europe, where demand grew rapidly before the accessory reached North America and became part of everyday clothing.

ALSO READ | Why People Are Soaking Their Feet In Vinegar And Salt – Does It Really Work?

Bandana History

The bandana gradually moved beyond practical use to represent different communities and causes. Cowboys wore it for protection against dust and heat, while African and Afro-descendant women in the Caribbean used headscarves to express cultural identity. In colonial Louisiana, Black women transformed head coverings imposed under the Tignon Laws into symbols of dignity and resilience. During the early 20th century, red bandanas became associated with labour movements in the United States, particularly during the 1921 Battle of Blair Mountain. Rosie the Riveter later made the red polka-dot bandana an enduring image of women's empowerment during World War II.

ALSO READ | Japan PM’s 3-Hour Sleep Routine: What It Could Be Doing To Her Brain

Celebrity Bandana Trend

The bandana continued evolving through the Chicano Movement, the LGBTQ+ community's Hanky Code, and later social justice campaigns, where it reflected identity and solidarity. It also became a signature accessory for musicians including Jimi Hendrix, Elvis Presley, Axl Rose, Bruce Springsteen, Willie Nelson, Madonna, Cher, 2Pac, Snoop Dogg, Amy Winehouse and Christina Aguilera. Today, celebrities such as Priyanka Chopra, Alia Bhatt, Katrina Kaif, Kiara Advani, Kareena Kapoor and Ananya Panday have brought the accessory back into mainstream fashion, proving that its appeal extends far beyond changing trends.

Few fashion accessories have travelled as far or carried as many meanings as the bandana. From India's textile heritage to modern celebrity wardrobes, it continues to blend history, culture and personal expression in a way that has kept it relevant for generations.

articles.title: You're probably using aluminium foil wrong: 9 Everyday mistakes that affect food quality and storage
articles.description: Aluminium foil sits in almost every Indian kitchen drawer, pulled out for everything from wrapping rotis and parathas to lining tandoor trays and covering leftover sabzi. It is affordable, easy to use, and endlessly adaptable, which is exactly why most of us never stop to think about whether we are actually using it the right way. But foil is not a one-size-fits-all solution, and a surprising number of everyday habits around it can quietly compromise food safety, taste, and shelf life. From reheating shortcuts to storage myths passed down through generations, here are nine common aluminium foil mistakes that could be affecting your food without you even realising it.
